nameStory: The genus name Boraria comes from the Greek word 'boros' meaning 'devouring' or 'gluttonous,' referring to millipedes' role as decomposers that constantly munch through leaf litter. The species name 'stricta' means 'straight' or 'upright' in Latin, likely describing this millipede's relatively rigid body posture compared to other more flexible species.
description: Boraria stricta is a flat-backed millipede, part of the cherry millipede family known for their flattened appearance and bright warning colors. These millipedes are decomposers that spend their lives crawling through leaf litter and soil, breaking down dead plant material. Like all millipedes, they have two pairs of legs per body segment (unlike centipedes which have one pair), giving them their characteristic slow, wave-like movement. They're relatively small creatures that you're more likely to find by carefully searching through forest debris than spotting in the open.

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: The body appears noticeably flattened from top to bottom rather than cylindrical, giving it a somewhat ribbon-like appearance when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Segment pattern
idTips.description: Each body segment has distinctive side extensions called paranota that create a ridged, armored look along the edges

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Moves with a slow, rhythmic wave motion as legs work in coordinated sequence - much slower than the quick darting of centipedes

idTips.label: Defensive behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, coils into a tight spiral and may release a mild chemical odor that smells faintly medicinal or almond-like

idTips.label: Texture when handled
idTips.description: Feels smooth and somewhat rigid to the touch, not squishy or soft like a worm - the exoskeleton provides a firm shell-like protection

habitat: Look for Boraria stricta in deciduous and mixed forests with rich, moist soil and deep leaf litter layers. They prefer areas under fallen logs, beneath thick accumulations of decomposing leaves, or in the soft humus layer where oak, maple, and beech trees drop their annual leaf fall. These millipedes need consistent moisture, so they're most common in sheltered forest floors rather than exposed or dry areas.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms and becomes workable, often found under logs and in fresh leaf litter from the previous fall. This is when they emerge from deeper winter shelters.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid periods, retreating deeper into soil or under cover during hot, dry spells. Best found in early morning when moisture levels are highest.
seasonality.fall: Very active as fresh leaf litter provides abundant food sources. Often seen crawling on the surface during damp autumn days as they process newly fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Dormant deeper in soil or under thick insulating layers of leaves and logs. Rarely visible unless you dig into protected microhabitats on warmer winter days.

funFact: Despite having 'milli' in their name meaning thousand, millipedes never actually have 1,000 legs - the most any species has is around 750, and most have far fewer, but they're still the leggiest creatures you'll encounter in New England forests!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with centipedes, but remember the simple rule: millipedes are 'mellow' with two pairs of legs per segment and slow movement, while centipedes are 'crabby' with one pair per segment and lightning-fast reflexes. Millipedes curl up defensively while centipedes bite and run.
contextualKnowledge: The common name 'cherry millipede' for this family can be misleading - it doesn't refer to the fruit, but rather to the cherry-red warning colors displayed by many species in this group, though not all family members are brightly colored.
compareHints: Since Boraria stricta is the only member of its genus found in New England, compare it to other flat-backed millipedes in the cherry millipede family. It tends to be less colorful than some of its flashy relatives that display bright reds, oranges, or yellows as warning colors. The 'stricta' species maintains a more subdued coloration while sharing the same flattened body plan and defensive chemical secretions that characterize this distinctive millipede family.
